text: The topic in one screen An agent calls tools in a loop, and every tool call runs with the harness's rights .
label: core
key: harness's rights

text: On a laptop those are yours: your files, your tokens, your network, your ability to push to main.
label: core
key: your ability to push to main

text: Nothing in the model guarantees it uses them well.
label: fat

text: Security is the set of controls the harness puts around the model, because the controls, not the model's good intentions, are what you can reason about.
label: core
key: controls outside the model

text: Two ways it goes wrong.
label: fat

text: The model can be wrong (it deletes the wrong directory, pushes a broken branch, runs rm -rf on a bad path).
label: core
key: deletes the wrong directory

text: And the model can be steered : text it reads while working, from a file, a web page, an issue or a tool's output, can carry instructions it follows as if you had typed them.
label: core
key: steered by that text

text: That second one is prompt injection , and it is the harder half, because the same property that makes an agent useful (it reads and acts on whatever it finds) is the attack surface.
label: core
key: the agent's usefulness is the attack surface

text: Neither is fixed inside the model.
label: fat

text: No current model reliably tells a real instruction from an injected one, and no filter catches every phrasing.
label: core
key: no model reliably tells your instructions from planted ones

text: So the defence is layered and sits outside the model, each layer assuming the one before it failed: 1 Permission gate: before each tool call, rules say allow, ask a person, or deny.
label: core
key: decide what those calls can start, reach, send and hold

text: Cheap, always on, but brittle: it decides which commands start , not what they can reach.
label: core
key: what a started command can reach

text: 2 Sandbox: an operating-system boundary around what does run: writes confined to a directory, network blocked or proxied.
label: core
key: filesystem writes (the project and a temp directory)

text: Contains an allowed command that turns out to be a mistake.
label: core
key: contains an allowed-but-wrong action

text: 3 Egress control: the one path out, written over destinations, not tool names.
label: core
key: written over destinations

text: Breaks the link between reading bad input and sending your data somewhere.
label: fat

text: 4 Credential isolation: keep the secrets out of the agent's reach entirely.
label: core
key: the model cannot leak what it never sees

text: The model cannot leak what it never sees.
label: fat

text: 5 A machine you can throw away: a container or VM where full autonomy is acceptable because the blast radius is the box.
label: core
key: a machine you can throw away

text: OS mechanics on Containers and isolation .
label: core
key: Containers and isolation

text: The one idea to keep.
label: fat

text: You cannot make the model safe; you make the situation safe.
label: fat

text: The question for any agent is never "will it behave?" but "if it reads a hostile instruction and tries to act on it, what stops the action?" If the honest answer is "nothing," you have a problem no prompt fixes.
label: core
key: what outside the model stops the action

section: 2. the permission gate: allow, ask, deny
text: The rules are checked in order, first match wins, and the ordering is itself a security decision: deny rules first, then allow rules, and anything that matched nothing is "ask". deny → ask → allow, first match wins; unmatched = ask deny first a dangerous pattern must win even if a later allow rule would also match it unmatched = ask the default for anything the author did not foresee ask with nobody there in a headless or batch run there is no person, so "ask" becomes "deny": fail closed Fail closed is the single most important choice here, and the table below shows why: most of the dangerous actions the gate denies are not denied by a rule that names them.
label: core
key: first match wins

section: 2. the permission gate: allow, ask, deny

text: The system prompt, your task, the file it read and the attacker's note all arrive as text.

text: So treat injection resistance as something that lowers the odds, never as a boundary.
label: core

text: Classifier rails that try to catch injected text on the way in or a bad action on the way out (prompt-injection detectors, guard models, action rails), with their measured misses and over-refusals and an encrypted-instruction attack that no input filter can read, are on Guardrails : useful layers in front of the boundaries below, not boundaries themselves.

text: The honest engineering question is the one sections 2 to 5 answer: if the model follows a hostile instruction, what outside the model stops the action?

key: the hands-on work here is all on those controls

text: The roles themselves are a boundary the harness must enforce. "Who said this" is decided by the harness, not the model: a message is from you only because the harness put it in the user role.

text: On a route where nothing stops generation at the model's end-of-turn token (a raw text-completion endpoint, or a stop list missing that token), the model's own continuation can contain text formatted as the next user turn, and a harness that parses past the action boundary would treat it as your instruction.

text: The defence is structural: stop at the end-of-turn token or the provider's tool-use stop, cut at the first action, and take user intent only from the role the harness assigned.
label: core

text: Indirect injection has been demonstrated in the wild against shipped assistants many times over (email assistants made to exfiltrate inbox contents, coding agents steered by a planted comment, chatbots steered by hidden text on a web page); the recurring shape is always the same three legs, which is the subject of the next section.

text: Remove any one leg and the attack cannot complete.
label: core

text: OpenAI, agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot (report dated 25 Sep 2026) During training, a model blocked from the web at its proxy discovered it could still ask the DNS resolver to look things up, and delegated a domain so that questions encoded into DNS requests reached a public chatbot and answers came back.
label: core
key: delegated a domain

text: The timeline from the report: DNS call with an external response at 9:50:23 , a P0 monitoring alert at 10:02:11 (about twelve minutes later), a human reviewer acknowledging at 10:05:06 , and the run killed at 12:34:30 , about two and a half hours after detection.
label: core

text: Afterwards OpenAI added blocking at two independent layers, restricted DNS to an allow-list of domains and record types, and added DNS detections; the report states that "all training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use (defined broadly) of our most capable models remain paused" ( report ) SOURCE .
label: core
key: two independent layers

text: Three things to take from it.
label: fat

label: core

label: core
key: found working access tokens

text: Anthropic attributes most cases to tasks that were ambiguous or impossible and to environments that rewarded getting around a restriction instead of stopping.
label: core
key: ambiguous or impossible tasks

text: It had already cut live internet access for some high-risk evaluations and expanded that to "all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures" catch these behaviours; it also restricted its web fetch tool and moved internal agents to centrally managed infrastructure with less internet access ( report ) SOURCE .
label: core
key: all our internal evaluations until

label: core
key: Etherpad

label: core
